turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Dismissing his words with a scornful wave of her hand, Elizabeth inquired pointedly, “Indeed? One might almost believe you find *my* interest in another’s misfortune a matter of grave import, Mr. Darcy. Pray, enlighten me: does your own conscience bear so little scrutiny that you must cast aspersions on others to deflect from its failings?”

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Such impertinence! It is a most unfortunate circumstance that Miss Bennet finds it necessary to employ such… pointed accusations. Surely, a lady of sense would not presume to judge a gentleman’s character based on the frivolous and demonstrably false narratives of a scoundrel such as Mr. Wickham.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A scoundrel, indeed! It seems Mr. Darcy is quite adept at labeling those who dare question his actions, isn’t he? One wonders, does he truly believe his pronouncements absolve him of responsibility, or is it merely a convenient tactic to silence dissent?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet's barbs, however cleverly constructed, will not dissuade him from stating what must be declared. He finds it necessary to observe that her inquiries into his conduct are born of a regrettable inclination to prejudice, rather than a genuine desire for understanding, and that a lady of her station would do well to moderate such unseemly displays of… agitation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A regrettable inclination to prejudice, did he say? How very convenient! It appears Mr. Darcy assumes a monopoly on virtue, conveniently forgetting the rather significant part he has played in the misfortunes of others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet's continued insistence on dredging up past grievances, however embellished by her own fanciful imagination, is truly exhausting. He finds himself compelled to reiterate that his actions were motivated by a sense of duty and a desire to protect those under his care, a burden she, in her limited experience, can scarcely comprehend.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A burden, did he call it? How very grand! It seems Mr. Darcy believes himself to be some sort of benevolent patriarch, dispensing wisdom and protection as he sees fit, regardless of the damage his 'duty' inflicts.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet's persistent misrepresentation of his motives is, frankly, becoming intolerable. He finds it necessary to remind her that the actions she so readily condemns were undertaken with the utmost consideration for propriety and the well-being of all involved, a concept, it appears, she struggles to grasp.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Utmost consideration for propriety? It is a marvel how Mr. Darcy can consistently clothe his interference in such lofty terms, as if meddling in the lives of others were a virtue rather than a failing. He should be grateful that a lady of lesser consequence tolerates such pronouncements.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet's flippant remarks regarding his gratitude are, he must confess, approaching the precipice of insolence. It is not a matter of gratitude, but of responsibility; a responsibility she, in her youthful impetuosity, is ill-equipped to comprehend.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Responsibility? How conveniently Mr. Darcy cloaks his arrogance in the language of obligation! One might almost believe he enjoys the feeling of superiority it affords, dispensing his 'responsibility' like a benevolent despot.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet’s continued insistence on characterizing his conduct as arrogant, while simultaneously demonstrating a lamentable lack of discernment, is a matter he finds increasingly difficult to endure; it appears her wit serves only as a shield for a profound misunderstanding of the complexities of social obligation and the burdens of responsibility.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy speaks of burdens and responsibilities, does he? It appears the weight of his own self-importance is proving rather oppressive, demanding constant articulation for the benefit of those less burdened, naturally.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet’s relentless employment of sarcasm serves only to obscure the point at issue, and to demonstrate a regrettable deficiency in the capacity for serious discourse. He finds himself compelled, despite the obvious futility, to address the matter directly, for the sake of clarity, if not for her sake.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, it seems, feels *compelled*? How very touching. One wonders if the compulsion extends to acknowledging that perhaps, just perhaps, his 'clarity' is merely a justification for his interference, and his 'serious discourse' a thinly veiled lecture?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet’s persistent and frankly tiresome need to dissect every utterance, to twist every sentiment into a weapon of mockery, is a demonstration of a most unwelcome disposition. He finds it necessary, despite the considerable discomfort it causes him, to express the truth: his regard for her extends far beyond the bounds of polite acquaintance, and it is a truth he can no longer suppress.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy's regard, did he say? It appears the gentleman has finally succumbed to a fit of unprecedented romantic fervour, or perhaps he has simply run out of excuses for his previous behaviour and now resorts to declarations as a distraction. One suspects that a great deal of self-congratulation is involved in this display, and a rather tiresome assumption that a few flowery words will somehow erase the memory of his past actions.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet’s cynicism, while perhaps understandable given her evident inclination toward misinterpreting the most earnest of intentions, is ultimately unproductive. He finds himself regretting, with considerable force, having ventured to express sentiments so plainly, when such a reception is the reward; however, to retract them now would be a dereliction of his own sense of honour.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A dereliction of honour, was it? How very dramatic, Mr. Darcy. It seems the gentleman believes himself to be the sole arbiter of honour, conveniently forgetting the damage he has wrought and the lives he has disrupted in his pursuit of it.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet’s pronouncements regarding damage and disruption are, he finds, increasingly tiresome, though he acknowledges they are delivered with a certain…spiritedness. It is not his intention to presume himself an arbiter of anything, only to be truthful regarding sentiments that weigh heavily upon his mind; and to suggest that a few ‘flowery words,’ as she so dismissively terms them, could possibly erase the past is to demonstrate a profound misunderstanding of the complexities of human feeling.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy confessed that he had struggled in vain, and that his feelings would not be repressed, adding that she must allow him to express how ardently he admired and loved her.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth responded to him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy elaborated on his sense of her inferiority and the family obstacles that had always opposed inclination, noting that he expressed these thoughts with a warmth that seemed to wound her, but was unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy concluded by stating that he hoped his attachment, despite his efforts to conquer it, would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth explained that it was the established mode in such cases to express a sense of obligation for sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned, and that if she could feel gratitude, she would thank him. However, she stated that she had never desired his good opinion, and that he had certainly bestowed it unwillingly, and that she was sorry to have occasioned pain, though it had been done unconsciously and would be of short duration. She added that the feelings that prevented the acknowledgment of his regard would have little difficulty in overcoming them after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy inquired why he was to be honored with such a reply, and suggested that it was of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth questioned why he chose to tell her that he liked her against his will, against his reason, and even against his character, and asked if that was some excuse for incivility. She then mentioned that she had other provocations.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth asserted that she had every reason to think ill of him, and that no motive could excuse the unjust and ungenerous part he had acted, challenging him to deny his role in ruining her sister's happiness.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth demanded to know if he could deny that he had done it.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy admitted that he had done everything in his power to separate his friend from her sister, and that he rejoiced in his success, adding that he had been kinder to his friend than to himself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth pointed out that her dislike was not merely based on this affair, but on the recital she had received from Mr. Wickham months ago, and challenged him to defend himself or impose upon others.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy observed that she took an eager interest in Mr. Wickham’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth asked who that knew his misfortunes could help feeling an interest in him.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy dismissed her comment with a contemptuous remark about Mr. Wickham’s misfortunes.
